title: Understanding Typography and How to Choose a Font
section: 12. Web Design School - Create a Website that People Love
summary: Font choice carries mood and affects readability. Explains serif versus sans-serif families and their sub-families, what makes type legible, and a simple pairing method: two fonts, similar mood and era, contrasting style or weight.

concepts.heading: Why typography matters
points: Fonts convey mood just as colours do; the wrong choice sends the wrong message (a cursive script on a serious message is her humorous example).
Pairing fonts well is one of the cheapest ways to make a design look polished.

concepts.heading: Serif family
points: Serifs are the small strokes (feet) at the ends of letter strokes. They are traditionally linked to carved stone lettering.
Mood: traditional, stable, respectable, authoritative, slightly old. Suited to legal letterheads, magazines, architecture and similar.

Sub-families: Old Style, Transitional, Modern, Slab Serif. A quick way to judge a serif's age is the contrast between the thickest and thinnest parts of a letter: low in Old Style, higher in Transitional, extreme in Modern.
Modern serifs (Didot is the example, as in a fashion magazine masthead) look authoritative yet contemporary; Old Style suits something aged, such as a winery.

concepts.heading: Sans-serif family
points: Sans-serif letters end in clean right angles with no feet.
Mood: friendly, approachable, contemporary, simple, straightforward. Popular with startups.
Humanist sans-serifs (Gill Sans, Tahoma, Verdana) are known for readability. Designers usually prefer sans-serif for body text.

A study on car dashboards found that switching from a Grotesque to a Humanist sans-serif cut the time drivers needed to read gauges by roughly 30-40%. The takeaway: legibility has measurable effects, and long copy that is easier to read is more likely to be read to the end.

concepts.heading: What makes a font legible
points: Open letter shapes with generous spacing between letters.
Unambiguous forms so similar characters are distinguishable (for example the letter g versus the digit 9).
Varied proportions, such as a wide capital O versus a narrower zero.

concepts.heading: Pairing rules
points: Use two fonts per design or per section; ten fonts look cluttered and amateur.
Pick fonts with a similar mood and from a similar era so they do not feel mismatched.
Create contrast through serif versus sans-serif (serif heading with sans body, or the reverse).
Create contrast through weight: a very bold or black heading with light, thin or regular body text.
She also shows six novelty fonts to avoid in professional work because they are hard to read and their moods are hard to fit; the fonts are shown on a slide and not named in the audio.

code_examples.caption: (Extra) A two-font pairing in CSS: serif heading, sans-serif body, contrasting weights

pitfalls: Using many fonts in one design.
Pairing fonts of clashing eras or moods.
Using decorative novelty fonts for body copy or professional sites.
Setting long body text in a font with tight spacing or ambiguous characters.
